claims.text: The proposed coating consists of alternating FCC CoCrFeMnNi layers and complementary BCC HEA layers.
The starting multilayer has pristine, sharp FCC/BCC interfaces at ambient conditions.
Severe lattice distortion and FCC/BCC interfacial misfit strain impede long-range dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocations accumulate in pile-ups at sharp FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial dislocation accumulation creates local stress concentrations and stress gradients.
Once a critical local stress is reached, interfacial resistance is overcome.
Exceeding the critical local stress activates interfacial slip.
Activated interfacial slip produces progressive plastic creep deformation under sustained loading.
Reducing individual layer thickness increases interface density.
Thinner layers will produce more pronounced interfacial dislocation pile-ups than thicker layers.
Thinner layers will produce higher local strain gradients than thicker layers.
Thinner-layer multilayers will creep faster than thicker-layer multilayers.
Thinner-layer samples will have lower effective yield strength than thicker-layer samples.
Plastic strain in thin-layer samples will be more localized at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Thicker-layer reference multilayers will show less dislocation accumulation and more uniform plastic flow.
At ambient temperature, thermal diffusion is minimal enough for the proposed multilayer mechanism to apply.
Elevated temperature, deformation twinning, or changes in short-range order may shift deformation away from the proposed mechanism.
Dislocation mechanisms are active during plastic deformation of BCC HEAs.
Stress and dislocation gradients can be associated with localized, gradient-mediated plastic deformation in compressed micropillars.
Interfacial dislocation accumulation, rather than cross-slip, recovery, or minor twinning, is the dominant source of creep in the proposed multilayer.
